did_you_know.text: Did you know? The chapter opens with a call to send a lamb or tribute from Sela in the wilderness to Mount Zion. This portrays an appeal to Jerusalem from a place of distress and sets Moab against Judah.

Did you know? Moab is asked to give the refugees shelter and protection—to hide the outcasts and be their shade at noonday. The image emphasizes their vulnerability and their urgent need for protection.

Did you know? In the midst of the distress, hope appears for a firmly established throne in the house of David. This rule is described as founded on steadfast love, truth, justice, and swift righteousness.

Did you know? The prophet presents Moab’s pride as a central cause of its condition: its pride, arrogance, and insolence are mentioned, along with the explanation that its boastful words will not help it.

Did you know? Moab’s destruction is also depicted through the devastation of its vineyards: the vine of Sibmah, the fields of Heshbon, and the branches that reached as far as Jazer are abandoned and ruined.

Did you know? Moab’s loss includes not only material destruction but also the loss of joy: there is no longer any singing in the vineyards, no treading in the winepresses, and the joyful shouts have ceased.
Did you know? The prophet expresses his grief through a musical image: his innermost being mourns for Moab like a harp. In this way, the lament takes on the sound of deep and unending inner sorrow.
Did you know? Even when Moab goes to its sanctuary to pray, it finds no power there to save it. The verse emphasizes the futility of worship in the face of the disaster described.
Did you know? The prophecy concludes with a clear time frame: within three years, measured like the years of a hired worker, Moab’s glory will be disgraced, and very little of it will remain.
